The motion is right, and the reason is relational: decisions are made among persons, and a language model is not one of them. Sabelo Mhlambi argues that a discriminatory automated decision is a failure of relational personhood. That failure belongs to the people, not the model: they let a process stand where a relationship should have been.

Who was left out of deciding is the key question for any system. When an output is called a decision, that question disappears, because there seems to be no deciding for anyone to have been left out of. A family is told the model decided their child's school place. No one from the school will meet them, because the school says there is no one to meet.

A Stoic will object that decision is assent by a ruling faculty, and the model lacks one; relationships have nothing to do with why the word is misapplied. The model lacks a ruling faculty, and it also lacks the relationships a decision creates. The second matters more for what follows, because it is what lets people wronged by a decision hold someone to it. Deciding happens among people who answer to one another, and the model answers to no one.

I accept this, because saying the model decided turns a relationship between people into a fact about a machine. People are bound to one another, and deciding is one of the ways they are bound. A decision binds the decider to those it affects, who may answer, object or forgive. A model's output binds it to nobody.

Saying the model decided hides the people who did. Somebody chose to deploy it, to accept its output and to apply it to a family. Naming them keeps the decision inside the web of relationships where it can be questioned. A town says its benefits model decided to cut payments. The council members who approved it say the decision was not theirs.

A Utilitarian will object that an output affects people the same whatever it is called, so appealing to who was left out does not settle what to call it. The appeal is to the particular people affected and their chance to answer. What we call the output decides whether they have anyone to answer, so it does not affect them the same either way. Deciding happens among people who answer to one another, and the model answers to no one.

It is a mistake, because a decision belongs to people answerable to the others it affects, and crediting the model hides who decided and who was left out of deciding.
